Well, a person might have a 'natural weight' in the sense that their height (mostly) and body structure (I'm talking broad shoulders vs small frame, for example, not "I naturally have a lot of fat on my body") determine their healthy weight.

OP, I think the phenomenon you're trying to describe is the result of how the body functions from an energy perspective. Everyone has a rate at which they expend energy strictly to stay alive. It's called the basal metabolic rate and it is the number of calories per day that someone's body burns in order to carry out basic, involuntary functions like digestion. It's dependent on the current state of the body, especially weight. A large person, tall man might have a BMR of 2500 calories a day. So, if he eats 2500 calories a day and does not exercise at all, then the difference between consumption and expenditure is zero. When there is no net difference, a person tends to maintain their weight. But, if he either eats 500 fewer calories per day OR burns 500 extra calories through exercise, he suddenly has a deficit of 500 calories. When the body operates at a deficit, it turns to fat stores to make up the difference--so routinely burning more than you consume will always cause weight loss, barring weird medical situations. (sorry if you already know all of this) The thing is, if the man in question loses 50 lbs doing this, then his new weight means that his body now needs less energy to operate normally. If he needed 2500 calories at 300 lbs and changed his diet so that he was eating only 2000 for a while and lost that weight, maybe now he only needs 2200 calories to function and maintain his weight. If he's still eating 2000 at this point, then the weight will be coming off more slowly because the deficit is now only 200 calories per day (as a rule of thumb, a pound of fat is equivalent to about 3500 cal). Some people don't realize that they need to be adjusting their diet after significant weight loss. Essentially you have more leeway when you're very overweight than when you just have a few pounds to lose. (this is the way I understand it, at least; if anyone sees any errors please let me know)

BUT, unless someone can explain to me otherwise,  'hidden calories' is a ridiculous term. The energy on the label is what the drink contains (per serving,  of course). That's the energy you take in by drinking it and that's what your body has to burn to counteract it. No more,  no less.  That said,  you mentioned you're exercising, which is good of course,  but weight loss is much, much easier to attain by focusing on diet. If you don't eat it in the first place, you don't have to burn it off. At a certain height and weight, your body needs somewhere around a specific number of energy units a day. A pound of fat is ~3500 energy units,  so if you eat only a reduced amount of energy units a day you will already lose about a pound a week. Without having to exercise at all. Any workout you do on top of that would help you lose it faster and probably build some muscle.  P.S. Sorry for the rambling,  just trying to help out :)
